rationale: The four studies differ a lot in sequencing depth, 16S region and protocol, so the same genus can sit at very different relative-abundance levels in each study. That makes pooled RF splits mix batch signal with disease signal. This version converts each genus's relative abundance to a percentile rank within its own study, using study only to harmonize and never as a predictor. The goal is to put abundances on a common scale so the forest learns within-study enrichment and depletion patterns, which is what the within-study AUROC scores. I haven't run it here, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

Right now every OTU without a genus annotation is pooled into a single `g__` feature, whichever family it belongs to. That mixes unrelated taxa, such as unclassified Enterobacteriaceae and unclassified Lachnospiraceae, and discards the family-level signal that matters most for IBD (loss of Ruminococcaceae/Lachnospiraceae, gain of Enterobacteriaceae). This change groups OTUs by their full lineage at both the family and genus levels, so unannotated genera stay separate within their own family. Each feature is then percentile-ranked within its study, as in the current best version.

IBD is consistently linked to lower gut diversity, but a random forest can't easily rebuild Shannon diversity or richness from hundreds of separate per-taxon ranks. This change adds explicit alpha-diversity features: Shannon and inverse Simpson at OTU and genus level, evenness, and richness estimated at a common read depth within each study so sequencing depth doesn't distort it. Like the taxa, each one is percentile-ranked within its own study, so the forest can split directly on reduced diversity. I haven't run this version, so it has no Dev score yet.

Family and genus lineages together give many very rare taxa. After per-study ranking, a taxon that is almost always zero is close to one constant value, so it is mostly noise. Those features dilute the random forest's random sqrt(p) feature subsets, so the informative IBD taxa get picked less often at each split. This change adds a label-free prevalence filter in `featurize`: a taxon is kept only if it is present (non-zero) in at least 10% of samples in at least one study. Taxa that are common in only one study (for example because of differences in 16S region or OTU sets) still survive.

Add an L2 logistic regression on the same per-study ranked family and genus features, and average its predictions with the random forest's by rank. IBD's main signals are steady, one-direction shifts across many taxa (loss of Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, Ruminococcaceae and Lachnospiraceae; gain of Enterobacteriaceae). A linear model adds these up smoothly while the forest catches interactions, and I pick its regularisation strength by inner grouped cross-validation using the training subject IDs.

The pooled forest is probably dominated by the largest study (Gevers RISK), and each study has a different case/control ratio. That lets the small adult studies, which differ in region and protocol, contribute little to the splits, yet the score is AUROC within each study. This change reweights training samples so that every (study × class) cell carries equal total weight. Study is used only to balance the training data, never as a predictor.

Gevers et al. 2014 published a microbial dysbiosis index for this kind of data. It is log(Enterobacteriaceae + Pasteurellaceae + Veillonellaceae + Fusobacteriaceae + Neisseriaceae + Gemellaceae) minus log(Bacteroidales + Clostridiales + Erysipelotrichaceae + Bifidobacteriaceae). A forest has trouble rebuilding a pooled log-ratio like this from hundreds of separately ranked taxa, so this change computes it explicitly, ranks it within each study and adds it as a feature. The final score blends the within-study rank of the forest's prediction with the within-study rank of the index. The blend weight comes from the forest's out-of-bag within-study AUROC on the training fold, and it can be 0 if the index doesn't help. I haven't run this version, so it has no Dev score yet.

IBD dysbiosis shows up as broad shifts at high taxonomic levels: Proteobacteria and Gammaproteobacteria go up, while Clostridia and Clostridiales go down. Higher-level labels are also assigned more consistently than genus labels across the four studies' different 16S regions and protocols. This change adds phylum, class and order lineage features alongside family and genus, ranked within each study as before, so the forest can split directly on these robust aggregate signals.

The IBD signal is spread thinly across hundreds of correlated, nested lineage features. With the default sqrt(p) features per split (about 3% of features), many splits may never see a strong taxon, and that could make the forest noisier. This change picks `max_features` from {sqrt, 0.05, 0.15, 0.3} on the training fold only. It scores each choice by the forest's out-of-bag AUROC within each study, which mirrors the harness metric without touching test data. The winning forest is used to predict, and I haven't run it, so there is no Dev score yet.

Right now zeros inside a study all share one tied percentile, so "absent" lands on a different value in each study: about 0.4 where 80% of samples are zeros, about 0.05 where 10% are. A taxon that never appears in a study (for example because that study used a different 16S region) gets 0.5 everywhere, which looks like middling abundance. This change encodes absence as 0 in every study and ranks only the non-zero samples within each study onto (0,1]. The order within each study is unchanged, but presence, absence and abundance now line up across studies, so pooled forest splits stop mixing detection differences between batches with disease signal. I haven't run it, so there is no Dev score for it yet.

I'm adding an ExtraTrees model and averaging its probabilities with the current random forest's, keeping everything else the same. The IBD signal is spread thinly over hundreds of nested, correlated lineage features with tied zeros. ExtraTrees' random split thresholds should smooth that noise and lower variance, and the two models' errors should only partly overlap, so the average should rank samples within each study more stably than the forest alone. I haven't run it, so there is no Dev score yet.

I'm replacing within-sample relative abundance with robust CLR (log counts minus the per-sample mean log over non-zero taxa only, done separately at each taxonomic level). Zeros stay tied at the bottom, and every feature is still percentile-ranked within its study. In IBD, blooms such as Enterobacteriaceae squeeze all other proportions down, so relative-abundance ranks mix that crowding effect with real depletion. Robust CLR ranks each taxon against the sample's typical non-zero taxon instead. That should separate true loss of Faecalibacterium, Roseburia and Clostridiales from that crowding, without pseudocounts that would depend on sequencing depth. I haven't run this version, so it has no Dev score yet.

This adds a label-aware dysbiosis-distance feature, following Halfvarson 2017's idea of measuring how far a sample sits from healthy reference samples. It is computed inside `fit_predict` from the training fold only: for each sample, the median L1 distance on the within-study-ranked features to that study's training controls, and separately to its training cases. Distances are computed at genus level, at family level and across all levels. For training samples, the sample itself and other samples from the same subject are left out. The forest can't build this whole-community "distance from a healthy gut" signal from separate taxon splits, and because the reference set is per study it stays harmonized across studies. I haven't run this version, so it has no Dev score yet.

IBD is heterogeneous (Crohn's vs UC, ileal vs colonic, on treatment or not). So the median distance to all of a study's training cases blurs across subtypes, and an IBD sample that closely matches one subtype can still look "average". This change keeps the current median dysbiosis distances and adds local k-nearest-neighbour versions alongside them. For each sample, at genus level, family level and across all levels, it takes the mean L1 distance to its k closest training controls from the same study and to its k closest training cases, plus their difference. Same-subject samples stay excluded, and k ≈ √(size of the reference set), clipped to 3–15. I haven't run this version, so there is no Dev score for it yet.

Add an out-of-fold, signature score that is consistent across studies. For each taxon, compute the effect size (Cohen's d, case minus control) separately within each study on the ranked features, then average across studies. Score each sample by the effect-weighted sum of its features at genus level and across all levels. Training rows are scored with grouped inner folds, so a row's own label never feeds its score. This gives the forest one smooth axis for the IBD shift that the studies share, which per-taxon splits and unsupervised distances only approximate.

I'm adding Bray-Curtis dysbiosis distances alongside the existing rank-L1 ones. For each sample, the new features are the median Bray-Curtis distance on relative abundance to that study's training controls and cases, at genus and family level. The current L1 distance on percentile ranks counts every taxon equally, including rare ones. Bray-Curtis is weighted by abundance, so it is driven by shifts in dominant taxa, such as loss of Faecalibacterium or Bacteroides and blooms of Enterobacteriaceae. That is the beta-diversity measure Halfvarson 2017 used to track IBD dysbiosis. Because the reference set comes from the same study and the features are standardized within each study, they stay harmonized across studies. Relative abundances are only used for these distances and are not passed to the random forest as features. I haven't run this version, so it has no Dev score yet.

This adds unweighted, presence/absence dysbiosis distances alongside the existing rank-L1 and Bray-Curtis ones: the median Jaccard distance to the same study's training controls and cases, at genus and family level. To keep sequencing depth from deciding what counts as "present", reads are first subsampled within each study, with a fixed seed, to that study's 10th-percentile read depth; samples below that depth keep all their reads. IBD involves loss of many low-abundance taxa, but neither abundance-weighted Bray-Curtis nor tied-zero ranks capture this well, and the earlier richness features (round 3) failed when added as standalone ranks, so this tries the same biology in the within-study distance form that has worked.

IBD dysbiosis appears as the coordinated loss or gain of whole guilds of co-abundant genera. One example is the butyrate-producer group of Faecalibacterium, Roseburia and Ruminococcaceae. A forest picking from hundreds of noisy, separately ranked genera only partly reconstructs these groups. This change adds label-free co-abundance module features. It clusters prevalent genera by their within-study-centred rank correlation and scores each module as the mean member rank, re-ranked within study. That gives the forest smoother features that are consistent across studies and capture whole guild shifts. I haven't run this version, so it has no Dev score yet.

Keep the co-abundance modules from round 18 but cut the same genus dendrogram at three heights instead of one. Cutting at 1−corr = 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 gives tight sub-guilds, the current guilds and broad consortia, which matters because IBD depletes both specific butyrate-producer cores and wider Clostridiales consortia. Modules that come out identical at more than one height are kept only once.

Rounds 13, 16 and 18 all helped: within-study distances to training controls and cases, and the label-free guild modules. This change combines them by adding a fourth rank-L1 dysbiosis-distance block computed on the co-abundance module profile. IBD shifts whole guilds together (butyrate producers down, Proteobacteria-linked guilds up), so a distance measured in guild space should be less noisy than one spread over hundreds of individual genus ranks.
